table.text: We conducted two behavioral studies with samples recruited on Prolific (https://prolific.com/).
table.formatted: We conducted two behavioral studies with samples recruited on Prolific (<ref type="url" target="https://prolific.com/">https://prolific.com/</ref>).

table.text: We recruited 340 participants in Study 1 and 300 in Study 2.
Participants were aged 18 to 80 (mean 42.7) in Study 1 and 19 to 79 (mean 40.9) in Study 2.
Participants completed the experiment in a median of 12.4 minutes in Study 1 and 9.1 minutes in Study 2.
All procedures were approved by the NYU Institutional Review Board, and all participants provided informed consent before beginning the experiment.

In each game, participants were instructed to maximize their point earnings over 20 or 40 trials, depending on game type (two context, three context, and Bernoulli games had double the number of trials due to task complexity).
The participants had to choose between 5 lettered buttons on the screen by clicking the buttons.

In Study 1, the hint was always present to the participant, and in Study 2, the hint was made visible only after a predetermined number of choices, altering the amount of prior experiential learning the subject had before being given a hint.

power.title: Power Analysis Check

table.text: We recruited 340 participants in Study 1 and 300 in Study 2. Participants self-reported their gender, which was not analyzed (Study 1: 176 men, 157 women, 3 preferred not to say, 1 other; Study 2: 140 men, 157 women, 2 preferred not to say, 1 other). Sample sizes were not determined by an a priori power analysis. A simulation-based sensitivity analysis (Section 4.6 and Appendix D) indicates that our design afforded 80% power to detect task-level hint effects of 2.1 to 10.6 percentage points of the arm spread depending on task. Minimum detectable effects for individual hints ranged from 2.2 to 13.3 percentage points, and for individual hint-by-onset conditions in Study 2 from 3.8 to 8.9.

Two of the four task-level effects reported as reliable in the main text exceeded their task's MDE, while two fell just below it (7.1 observed against an MDE of 7.4 for two context, and 10.4 against 10.6 for linear contextual), and we accordingly treat their magnitudes as approximate. The MDEs also indicate that only large hint benefits were reliably detectable in the drifting, three context, and Bernoulli tasks, so the lack of aggregate hint effects (see Results in the main text) should not rule out the possibility of moderate effects. At the per-hint level, 12 of the 13 significant effects (starred conditions in Fig. 4) exceeded their specific MDE. The remaining one was still detected despite an observed magnitude below its 80%-power threshold, as true effects below the MDE may still be detected with lower probability. This implies that this estimate of a hint effect is more susceptible to magnitude overestimation, as when power is low, the detected experiments are more likely to have noise inflation. We interpret this effect, the harmful structure hint in the Bernoulli task (observed 9.9 vs. MDE 10.8), whose direction is supported (p = .024), as evidence of effect direction rather than precise effect size.

report: Reporting *p* values imprecisely (e.g., *p* < .05) reduces transparency, reproducibility, and re-use (e.g., in *p* value meta-analyses). Best practice is to report exact p-values with three decimal places (e.g., *p* = .032) unless *p* values are smaller than 0.001, in which case you can use *p* < .001.

This module sometimes flags false positives when sentences discuss how p-value thresholds were set. It can also miss an imprecise p-value that is reported against a threshold (e.g., "decreased at the *p* < .05 significance threshold").

::: {.callout-tip title="Learn More" collapse="true"} The APA manual states: Report exact *p* values (e.g., *p* = .031) to two or three decimal places. However, report *p* values less than .001 as *p* < .001. However, 2 decimals is too imprecise for many use-cases (e.g., a *p* value meta-analysis), so report *p* values with three digits. American Psychological Association (2020). Publication manual of the American Psychological Association, 7 edition. American Psychological Association. :::

stat_p_nonsig.report: Meta-scientific research has shown nonsignificant p values are commonly misinterpreted. It is incorrect to infer that there is 'no effect', 'no difference', or that groups are 'the same' after p > 0.05. It is possible that there is a true non-zero effect, but that the study did not detect it. Make sure your inference acknowledges that it is possible that there is a non-zero effect. It is correct to include the effect is 'not significantly' different, although this just restates that p > 0.05. Metacheck does not yet analyze automatically whether sentences which include non-significant p-values are correct, but we recommend manually checking the sentences below for possible misinterpreted non-significant p values. ```{r} #| echo: false # table data -------------------------------------- table <- structure(list(Text = c("p > .1", "p = .086"), Sentence = c("For all other hints, the differences between onsets were not reliable (all p > .1).", "Removing the hierarchy cost very little overall (1.346 nats; per-participant difference 0.007 [-0.001, 0.015], p = .086), but this near-zero difference hides two opposing effects." )), row.names = c(NA, -2L), class = c("tbl_df", "tbl", "data.frame" )) # display table ----------------------------------- metacheck::report_table(table, c(0.1, 0.9), 10, FALSE) ``` ::: {.callout-tip title="Learn More" collapse="true"} For metascientific articles demonstrating the rate of misinterpretations of non-significant results is high, see: Aczel B, Palfi B, Szollosi A, Kovacs M, Szaszi B, Szecsi P, Zrubka M, Gronau Q, van den Bergh D, Wagenmakers E (2018). “Quantifying Support for the Null Hypothesis in Psychology: An Empirical Investigation.” Advances in Methods and Practices in Psychological Science, 1(3), 357–366. doi:10.1177/2515245918773742. Murphy S, Merz R, Reimann L, Fernández A (2025). “Nonsignificance misinterpreted as an effect’s absence in psychology: Prevalence and temporal analyses.” Royal Society Open Science, 12(3), 242167. doi:10.1098/rsos.242167. For educational material on preventing the misinterpretation of p values, see [Improving Your Statistical Inferences](https://lakens.github.io/statistical_inferences/01-pvalue.html#sec-misconception1). :::

data_check.summary_text:
-  We classified 480 files: 304 data, 124 code, 16 documentation, 14 materials, 4 output, 18 unknown.
-  We found 92 tabular data files and extracted 1222 columns from 92 of them.
-  We grouped the files into 2 study groups (ex1, ex2), plus 4 collection-level files (README/ro-crate metadata). We ran automated data-quality checks on 1222 columns; 60 columns have at least one potential issue (48 columns with no observed values (entirely empty); 8 columns of free text that may contain personal detail; 4 columns whose name suggests personal information).

:::

This module runs automated data-quality checks (empty columns, SPSS filter variables, category casing, stray whitespace, numbers stored as text, problematic and colliding column names, mixed text encodings, personal information, spreadsheet formatting, and careless responding) on the extracted data files.
We examined 1222 columns across 92 data files.
#### Issues Identified

60 file/column combinations have at least one issue.

**About the personal-information flags.** These are pattern matches, not confirmed disclosures, and they are tuned to over-report rather than miss something. Expect false positives:

- **Column names** are matched against identifying words in English and other European languages (`email`, `telefoonnummer`, `geboortedatum`, ...). A column called `phone_number` flags whether or not it holds one, and an empty or already-anonymised column flags on its name alone.
- **Values** are matched against the shape of an identifier. An IP address pattern also matches a version string or a dotted numeric code; a card-number pattern requires both a real issuer prefix and a checksum, but a long numeric ID can still coincide.
- **Free text** is flagged when a column holds long, mostly-distinct prose — the shape open-ended answers take. Most such columns contain no names at all.

A flag means *look at this column*. Where the data is already de-identified (an `ip` column reading `Anonymized`, a `name` column the authors emptied), no action is needed.

#### Careless Responding
No file could be screened for careless responding.

**What this does not cover.** Only 0 of 92 data files could be screened: the rest had no detectable multi-item scale block, or too few respondents. Even in a screened file, these checks only look at multi-item rating scales — the only place where a repeated or flat answer pattern is interpretable. Single questions, open text, demographics and any item outside a detected scale block are never examined. A respondent can therefore answer most of a survey carelessly and still not be flagged here, and finding nothing is not evidence that a dataset is free of careless responding.

summary_table.ethics_statements: All procedures were approved by the NYU Institutional Review Board, and all participants provided informed consent before beginning the experiment.
live_data_statements: Consistent with this, the patch foraging hint "Find a few good buttons and alternate between them to maximize your points" helped at trial 0 (6.2, [3.2, 9.3], p < .001) and remained beneficial when introduced as late as trial 12 (8.4, [2.9, 13.9], p = .029; Fig. 5c2), after participants had experienced the rewards depleting.
We conducted two behavioral studies with samples recruited on Prolific (https://prolific.com/).
We recruited 340 participants in Study 1 and 300 in Study 2.
Participants were aged 18 to 80 (mean 42.7) in Study 1 and 19 to 79 (mean 40.9) in Study 2.
Participants completed the experiment in a median of 12.4 minutes in Study 1 and 9.1 minutes in Study 2.
All procedures were approved by the NYU Institutional Review Board, and all participants provided informed consent before beginning the experiment.

In each game, participants were instructed to maximize their point earnings over 20 or 40 trials, depending on game type (two context, three context, and Bernoulli games had double the number of trials due to task complexity).
The participants had to choose between 5 lettered buttons on the screen by clicking the buttons.

In Study 1, the hint was always present to the participant, and in Study 2, the hint was made visible only after a predetermined number of choices, altering the amount of prior experiential learning the subject had before being given a hint.

text.text: Humans acquire knowledge through two profoundly different routes: explicit instruction through language, and implicit experience accumulated through action.
How these sources reconcile to guide decisions is poorly understood.

To study their integration, we introduce the Instructed Bandit Tasks (IBT), eight sequential decision-making problems in which participants earn rewards while given natural-language hints conveying partial information about the task environments.
Across two large (N = 337 and N = 300) behavioral experiments, linguistic hints improved performance and systematically reshaped choice trajectories.

We propose modeling these effects with a hierarchical Bayesian RL agent, which treats language as a probabilistic constraint over beliefs, and compare it against Centaur, a language model fine-tuned on human behavior.
Both models predicted which hints improve learning, and Centaur additionally reproduced when language hurt performance or lost its benefit under additional experience.
Their complementary strengths suggest that normative and data-driven cognitive models can together capture the nuances of human learning.
Human decision making is influenced by at least two types of information, which each tug at the processes of deliberation and choice.
One, sometimes known as value-based decision making, is acquired through direct experience [1, 2], and is implicit, statistical, and accrued incrementally across time [3].
text.formatted: One, sometimes known as value-based decision making, is acquired through direct experience <ref type="bibr" target="#b0">[1,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b1">2]</ref>, and is implicit, statistical, and accrued incrementally across time <ref type="bibr" target="#b2">[3]</ref>.

text.text: The other, communicated rapidly and abstractly through language, is semantically rich, communicative, and often vague [4] [5] [6].
text.formatted: The other, communicated rapidly and abstractly through language, is semantically rich, communicative, and often vague <ref type="bibr" target="#b3">[4]</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b4">[5]</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b5">[6]</ref>.

text.text: Though seemingly distinct, language and direct experience are deeply integrated in everyday decision making and learning [7, 8].
text.formatted: Though seemingly distinct, language and direct experience are deeply integrated in everyday decision making and learning <ref type="bibr" target="#b6">[7,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b7">8]</ref>.

text.text: When deciding where to get coffee, for example, an individual can rely on their own past experiences at different cafes while also considering a recommendation of a friend that "Coffee Project is the best."
The integration of language with experiential learning is non-trivial, as these two sources rely on somewhat incommensurate cognitive processes and representations [9, 10].
text.formatted: The integration of language with experiential learning is non-trivial, as these two sources rely on somewhat incommensurate cognitive processes and representations <ref type="bibr" target="#b8">[9,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b9">10]</ref>.

text.text: Prior research has largely overlooked the direct integration of language and experience, in part due to the relative scarcity of theoretical frameworks for combining language with other forms of learning (but see [9] [10] [11]).
text.formatted: Prior research has largely overlooked the direct integration of language and experience, in part due to the relative scarcity of theoretical frameworks for combining language with other forms of learning (but see <ref type="bibr" target="#b8">[9]</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b9">[10]</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b10">[11]</ref>).

text.text: For instance, research on the "description-experience gap" has, in separate tasks, explored how experienced versus described gambles influence risky choice behavior [12] while leaving their integration relatively underexplored [8, 10].
text.formatted: For instance, research on the "description-experience gap" has, in separate tasks, explored how experienced versus described gambles influence risky choice behavior <ref type="bibr" target="#b11">[12]</ref> while leaving their integration relatively underexplored <ref type="bibr" target="#b7">[8,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b9">10]</ref>.

text.text: However, recent Centaur, a language model fine-tuned on human behavior, receives the same task instructions, hint, and history as text.
The Bayesian model combines the hint with priors over task types (τ ), arm means (µ) and taskspecific parameters (θ), and updates its beliefs after each choice and reward.

This paradigm yields choice trajectories for all three learners under each task condition. b) The three learners are compared on the effect on performance for each hint, hint effects based on timing, choice patterns, and fit to held-out human choices.
advances in AI, particularly the linguistic competence of large language models (LLMs), make capturing the influence of language on other types of processes more amenable to comprehensive study [13].
text.formatted: advances in AI, particularly the linguistic competence of large language models (LLMs), make capturing the influence of language on other types of processes more amenable to comprehensive study <ref type="bibr" target="#b12">[13]</ref>.

text.text: In this paper, we conceptualize the integration of language and experience in the form of "hints" provided to a learner during experiential learning.
Hints are a common form of language-based input, resembling the advice, tips, and recommendations that accompany everyday learning.

Like a friend's verbal hint on how to play a board game, hints need not convey the relative values of all options, carry explicit measures of confidence, or agree with the learner's own experience to be informative [8], and it is yet unknown how such partial descriptions of a problem influence decision making and choice.
text.formatted: Like a friend's verbal hint on how to play a board game, hints need not convey the relative values of all options, carry explicit measures of confidence, or agree with the learner's own experience to be informative <ref type="bibr" target="#b7">[8]</ref>, and it is yet unknown how such partial descriptions of a problem influence decision making and choice.

text.text: To understand how people integrate language and experience requires probing for the different effects language can have on choice behavior.

We establish a new approach to studying the integration process by augmenting a popular experimental learning paradigm, the multi-armed bandit (MAB) task [14, 15], with natural language hints to create a set of Instructed Bandit Tasks (IBT).
text.formatted: We establish a new approach to studying the integration process by augmenting a popular experimental learning paradigm, the multi-armed bandit (MAB) task <ref type="bibr" target="#b13">[14,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b14">15]</ref>, with natural language hints to create a set of Instructed Bandit Tasks (IBT).

text.text: In the IBT, learning agents receive a hint providing partially constraining information about the structure or parameters of a sequential decisionmaking task, make a series of choices, and observe evaluative feedback on those choices in the form of rewards (Fig. 1).
text.formatted: In the IBT, learning agents receive a hint providing partially constraining information about the structure or parameters of a sequential decisionmaking task, make a series of choices, and observe evaluative feedback on those choices in the form of rewards (Fig. <ref type="figure" target="#fig_0">1</ref>).

text.text: The hints guide learners towards better options or to adopt certain policies, vary in their informativeness, and are experimentally provided at different times to systematically interrogate the learning process.
In concert with our novel empirical task, we develop a theory of how language input reshapes a learner's world model by constraining their beliefs over the task structures [similar to 16].
text.formatted: In concert with our novel empirical task, we develop a theory of how language input reshapes a learner's world model by constraining their beliefs over the task structures [similar to <ref type="bibr" target="#b15">16]</ref>.

text.text: We model this via a hierarchical Bayesian reinforcement learning (RL) agent, in which natural language hints translate into functions which contribute an additional prior over the learning agent's belief states.

By modeling human choices across combinations of hints, task structures, and experimental conditions, we found that humans integrate natural language and experience in ways that reflect Bayesian principles, and that language models aligned to human behavior reproduce these tendencies.
This work provides a formal and more expansive account of how language and experience interact to guide choice.

To study the integration of language with experience, we added task-relevant natural language hints to variants of the multi-armed bandit.

MABs formalize sequential, value-based decisions under uncertainty, have been studied computationally in economics, optimization, and RL for several decades [2, 14, 15, 17], and are a popular framework for studying animal and human learning [18] [19] [20], since simple reward-maximizing tasks can be performed regardless of language competence.
text.formatted: MABs formalize sequential, value-based decisions under uncertainty, have been studied computationally in economics, optimization, and RL for several decades <ref type="bibr" target="#b1">[2,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b13">14,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b14">15,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b16">17]</ref>, and are a popular framework for studying animal and human learning <ref type="bibr" target="#b17">[18]</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b18">[19]</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b19">[20]</ref>, since simple reward-maximizing tasks can be performed regardless of language competence.

text.text: In the simplest case of a stationary N -armed bandit, a learning agent repeatedly chooses between N arms, each returning a reward sampled from a fixed Gaussian distribution with unknown mean µ and variance σ 2 , and must balance exploration, in observing the rewards from each arm, with exploitation, in choosing the arm with the highest expected reward [15].
text.formatted: In the simplest case of a stationary N -armed bandit, a learning agent repeatedly chooses between N arms, each returning a reward sampled from a fixed Gaussian distribution with unknown mean µ and variance σ 2 , and must balance exploration, in observing the rewards from each arm, with exploitation, in choosing the arm with the highest expected reward <ref type="bibr" target="#b14">[15]</ref>.

text.text: Building off of the stationary MAB, we study eight tasks which include bandit problems with non-stationary arm means (drifting, patch foraging), as when a favorite restaurant changes quality; context dependencies (two context and three context), as when the fastest route home depends on the day of the week; time dependencies (time delayed), as when effective changes in diet and exercise are only observed weeks later; alternative reward distributions (Bernoulli), as when one bus line proves more reliably on time than another; and feature dependencies (linear contextual), as when an apartment is judged by a renter's personalized priorities.
We selected this set from a survey of bandit varieties in the neuroscience, psychology, and human RL literature to span commonly studied dynamics.
We include formal definitions of the task types in Appendix A and Table A1.
text.formatted: We include formal definitions of the task types in Appendix A and Table <ref type="table">A1</ref>.

text.text: In contrast to standard MAB scenarios, language comprehension is critical in our Instructed Bandit Tasks.
In the IBT, the formulation of the problem and the agent's learning objective are fixed, but the agent additionally receives a natural language hint, such as "Arm 1 is greater than 25".
This hint provides only partial information, as it is uninformative about the relative values of the other arms.
If the learning agent effectively harnesses the information provided by the hint as a constraint over the problem space, then their choice behavior should change in a systematic and measurable way.

We created a custom set of hints for each task by conducting pilot studies with participants, the Centaur model (a language model fine-tuned on human behavior), and the Bayesian model and searching for hints which affected learning behavior.
This set should be understood as a sample of hints that can influence learning rather than a representative sample of all possible hints.
Each hint can also be roughly classified by whether it contributed information about the value of the arms (V), structure of the problem (S), or policy of the optimal solution (P).
The hints are single sentences and include placeholder references to the arm choices, as we rotated the position of the arms across the games to avoid numerical or positional biases.
Examples of each hint type are provided in Table 1 and the full dataset of hints is in Appendix B and Table A2.
text.formatted: Examples of each hint type are provided in Table <ref type="table">1</ref> and the full dataset of hints is in Appendix B and Table <ref type="table">A2</ref>.

text.text: We use the IBT to experimentally manipulate the integration of language and experience in humans through two large-scale studies.
Study 1 evaluated participants on all tasks and hints in the IBT.

Study 2 additionally manipulated the timing of the hint in two task types (stationary and patch foraging) to explore whether the amount of accumulated experience changes how participants integrate the information from language.
Implementation details for both behavioral experiments are in Section 4.1.
We characterize the integration process by comparing human behavior to two computational models which derive from contrasting assumptions about human learning (Fig. 1).
text.formatted: We characterize the integration process by comparing human behavior to two computational models which derive from contrasting assumptions about human learning (Fig. <ref type="figure" target="#fig_0">1</ref>).

text.text: The first is a hierarchical Bayesian reinforcement-learning agent that offers a normative account of the integration process by treating each hint as a prior constraint over the space of possible task representations (Fig. 2a) [4, 21, 22].
text.formatted: The first is a hierarchical Bayesian reinforcement-learning agent that offers a normative account of the integration process by treating each hint as a prior constraint over the space of possible task representations (Fig. <ref type="figure" target="#fig_1">2a</ref>) <ref type="bibr" target="#b3">[4,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b20">21,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b21">22]</ref>.

text.text: As the Bayesian model maintains explicit posteriors over task types, task parameters, and arm values, it is also highly interpretable and allows for inspection into how a hint changes its beliefs and actions at the individual trial level (Fig. 2b,c).
text.formatted: As the Bayesian model maintains explicit posteriors over task types, task parameters, and arm values, it is also highly interpretable and allows for inspection into how a hint changes its beliefs and actions at the individual trial level (Fig. <ref type="figure" target="#fig_1">2b</ref>,<ref type="figure">c</ref>).

text.text: For the second model, the integration of language and experience is emergent and data-driven.
Centaur is a large open-weight language model (Llama 3.1 70B base [24]) fine-tuned on a large-scale text corpus of psychological experiments [25].
text.formatted: Centaur is a large open-weight language model (Llama 3.1 70B base <ref type="bibr" target="#b23">[24]</ref>) fine-tuned on a large-scale text corpus of psychological experiments <ref type="bibr" target="#b24">[25]</ref>.

text.text: Centaur is argued to be a "foundation model" for human behavior, meaning it is able to capture a wide range of hints and natural language instructions without hand-engineering.
The operation of Centaur is more opaque, and its predictions are agnostic to the explicit model of the reward generating process in each task.
Its value is then less as an explanation than as a human choice simulator and a benchmark to identify the aspects of human learning that the formal cognitive model fails to capture [26].
text.formatted: Its value is then less as an explanation than as a human choice simulator and a benchmark to identify the aspects of human learning that the formal cognitive model fails to capture <ref type="bibr" target="#b25">[26]</ref>.

text.text: These two models, stemming from quite different traditions, thus provide complementary analyses of the integration of language and experience.
To study the integration of language and experience through the IBT, each task must be learnable.
Even without hints, we expect participants to show decreasing trial-by-trial average regret-or difference between the mean of the arm they chose and that of the optimal arm-over the game trials.

We normalized raw regret as a percentage of a game's arm value range, and report hint effects throughout as differences in this normalized regret, in percentage points, which makes them comparable across games and task types.

In the no-hint games, regret decreased significantly from the first to last five trials across all eight task types (Fig. 3a, purple curves; paired t-tests, t range 2.25-31.07, all Holm-adjusted p < .05, see Appendix C and Table A3), supporting the case that participants learn the reward structures of each task through experience alone.
text.formatted: In the no-hint games, regret decreased significantly from the first to last five trials across all eight task types (Fig. <ref type="figure" target="#fig_2">3a</ref>, purple curves; paired t-tests, t range 2.25-31.07, all Holm-adjusted p < .05, see Appendix C and Table <ref type="table">A3</ref>), supporting the case that participants learn the reward structures of each task through experience alone.

text.text: Because the hints in IBT are always true (they conveyed information about the actual parameters of the problem to avoid deception), an ideal Bayesian learner should use them to reduce uncertainty about the task and improve performance.
Accordingly, we computed the difference in average task regret between participants given a hint and those given no hint for each of the eight tasks.

Fig. 3b (purple bars) shows that participants who received a hint achieved lower mean regret throughout the games than those without in seven of eight task types (a mean relative reduction of 6.8% overall and 13.9% in the first five trials).

text.text: The hints which directly contributed information about the arm values most consistently improved participant performance.
As many of these value-based hints identified the best arm (e.g. "{max2} is the best."), they eliminated the need to search and reduced the decision problem to simple exploitation.
The strongest effect appeared in the time delayed environment, where the k-trial reward delay makes learning from experience challenging.
In this case, participants given "{max2} is the best." achieved a reduced regret of 24.5 percentage points ([16.7, 32.4], p < .001).
text.formatted: In this case, participants given "{max2} is the best." achieved a reduced regret of 24.5 percentage points ([16.7, 32.4], p < .001).

text.text: Notably, the hint was even more helpful to participants (reduced regret by 37.2 percentage points, [29.2, 45.2], p < .001) when it additionally referenced the task structure ("{max2} is the best, even if it doesn't seem like it at first.").

text.text: Large value-based hint effects were similarly observed in the stationary task ("{max2} is the best."), where regret reduced by 12.9 percentage points ([11.4, 14.5], p < .001), and in the Bernoulli task ("{max2} is most likely to return 100 points."), where regret reduced by 15.7 percentage points ([7.9, 23.5], p < .001).

text.text: Because some tasks shared the same hint, we could also see that a hint's effect varied with the task type even under fixed language. "{max2} is the best" was roughly twice as beneficial in the time delayed environment as in the stationary one.
This suggests that the amount of uncertainty a hint can resolve depends on the task structure and how much experience is required to learn its parameters.
When beliefs converge slowly, such as with delayed feedback, language may accomplish more inferential work.
Next, hints did not only substitute for evidence on arm values, but also guided learners toward more efficient search strategies.
In the patch foraging task, the hint "Find a few good buttons and alternate between them to maximize your points" reduced average regret by 5.9 percentage points ([4.0, 7.8], p < .001).
text.formatted: In the patch foraging task, the hint "Find a few good buttons and alternate between them to maximize your points" reduced average regret by 5.9 percentage points ([4.0, 7.8], p < .001).

text.text: Since the optimal strategy in a depleting-rewards environment is to rotate among top choices rather than exploit a single arm, participants evidently extracted the policy-level information from the hint and adapted their behavior accordingly.
Finally, in some cases, participants given certain hints performed significantly worse than those given no hint.

For example, in the patch foraging task, the hint "The points you get on the first pick of a button are the most representative of the button value" also reliably increased regret (hint effect of -3.0 percentage points, [-4.9, -1.0], p = .009).

As all hints in the IBT are designed to be helpful and to strictly contribute positive information, this demonstrates a case where ostensibly helpful linguistic information can actively mislead or distract from experiential learning.

To further investigate how people weigh linguistically-provided priors against accumulated reward experience, Study 2 varied the trial (0, 4, 8, or 12) at which a hint appeared relative to accumulated experience.

text.text: This indicates diminishing returns, as earlier hints incorporate easily into learning before strong behavioral tendencies form, whereas later hints may conflict with already-formed strategies and fail to update people's behaviors.
One exception is that the patch foraging hint "The points you get on the first pick of a button are the most representative of the button value." showed a surprising but opposite effect.
The hint undermined participant performance when introduced at trials 0 and 4 (reliably at trial 0, -4.6, [-7.7, -1.5], p = .029) and had a neutral effect when introduced in later trials (Fig. 5c4).

text.text: A possible explanation is that hints which change a participant's initial exploration strategy can prevent them from observing the evidence they need to learn, and become helpful only once some experience provides context for interpreting them.

Consistent with this, the patch foraging hint "Find a few good buttons and alternate between them to maximize your points" helped at trial 0 (6.2, [3.2, 9.3], p < .001) and remained beneficial when introduced as late as trial 12 (8.4, [2.9, 13.9], p = .029; Fig. 5c2), after participants had experienced the rewards depleting.

text.text: In summary of the behavioral studies, people were able to use hint information to improve performance, but the effect of any given hint varied with task structure, strictly true information could be detrimental, and the helpfulness of some hints depended on how much experience had yet accumulated.
A successful computational account must then capture these nuanced effects in fusing linguistic and experienced data to predict human choice.
First, we fit the hierarchical Bayesian agent and variants of the Centaur language model to the trial-level human choices.
We split the behavioral dataset from Study 1 by participant such that all trials from a given individual would appear in either the train or test set.
For all models, we fit the parameters globally across all game types and individuals.
Details of the model fitting and validation are described in Section 4.4.

text.text: Centaur's three largest advantages, of 7 to 17 percentage points, were all value hints identifying the best arm, which people acted strongly on and the Bayesian model underestimated.
The Bayesian model's advantages were smaller, 3 to 8 percentage points, and came from hints describing the task's structure or dynamics.

Of these eight differences, only the one for the linear contextual hint "If the third number under the button is 1, you will get the most points." was reliably different from zero on its own, so we read the split as a consistent pattern across hints rather than as eight separate findings.
The Bayesian model fits human choices slightly less well than Centaur.

However, the Bayesian model, provided the generative structure of the eight task types and a hand-specified meaning function for each hint, gives a normative account of the integration of language and experience with only two fitted parameters (T and γ).

Centaur, which receives only the text of the task, hint, and history and has one fitted parameter (β), proves to be highly predictive of human choice patterns yet does not explain how these information sources combine.
The two models thus serve as complementary tools for understanding how language shapes human experience and learning.
Language and direct experience both contribute to the decisions we make.
In this paper, we explore if there are coherent principles that guide their integration.
We created a novel setting, the Instructed Bandit Tasks, to systematically study how people use language while learning from experience.
The hints we studied occupy a different niche than the informationally equivalent descriptions studied in the description-experience gap [12] literature.
text.formatted: The hints we studied occupy a different niche than the informationally equivalent descriptions studied in the description-experience gap <ref type="bibr" target="#b11">[12]</ref> literature.

text.text: In our setting, verbal descriptions were partial, arrived amid ongoing experience, and more closely resembled the advice and tips that accompany everyday learning.

We found that hints differed in helpfulness under different task types, hints that were strictly true sometimes made learners reliably worse, and the same hint could help at one point and have no effect at another depending on how much experience the learner had accrued.
These effects suggest that natural language does not contribute a fixed amount of information into the learning process, but instead reshapes a learner's hypothesis space of the current task world.
From this view, the function of language in learning is to reshape the learner's world model and reweight their task representations.
We attempted to capture this by constructing a hierarchical Bayesian agent which encodes the semantics of each hint as a secondary prior weighting of its beliefs.

The Bayesian framing then offers a normative account of the integration process, as both linguistic and experienced evidence are cast into the common currency of probability and combined via Bayes' rule.
The fitted Bayesian model captured which hints help and in which tasks, and was highly interpretable, allowing us to trace in time as a learner's beliefs changed about the nature of the task.
One limitation of this approach is the manual curation of the hints and meaning functions, which ablations show account for most of the model's fit (Appendix G and Fig. A2).
text.formatted: One limitation of this approach is the manual curation of the hints and meaning functions, which ablations show account for most of the model's fit (Appendix G and Fig. <ref type="figure" target="#fig_1">A2</ref>).

text.text: One way to address this is to use LLMs to translate arbitrary natural language inputs into these formal constraints, in the spirit of the model synthesis architectures [16], which would also scale the approach beyond the set of hints studied here.

text.text: A central contribution of our paper is to compare this Bayesian account to that of a fine-tuned large language model.

Fit only by rescaling its choice distributions, Centaur assigned the highest likelihood to the held-out human choices and reproduced the fine-grained behavioral signatures of the human data with highest fidelity, despite never having been trained on IBT (though Psych-101 includes other bandit tasks) or optimized for these metrics.

Most notably, while the normative Bayesian agent captured cases where language reduces uncertainty in a verifiable way, Centaur reproduced human errors, such as when informative hints harmed performance and when the benefit of a hint faded with experience.

That a model trained only to predict the next token of human choice sequences is able to predict the cases in which humans will act suboptimally supports that Centaur has implicitly learned the behavioral regularities of how language governs experiential learning in humans.
These approaches capture opposite sides of growing debates about approaches to cognitive modeling.
Our results suggest that they might not be so incommensurate.
There was significant alignment between Centaur and the Bayesian model in terms of prediction (r = 0.85 across hint effects; Section 2.4).

The two models can also be used together in the spirit of scientific regret minimization [26], in which the cases where a predictive model like Centaur succeeds and a normative model fails identify revisions for the latter.

Future work could test hints that are conflicting or wrong (as everyday advice often is) and which an account of language as world-model constraint predicts should mislead learners in equally systematic ways (cf. ref. [10]).

text.text: As everyday advice often comes from speakers of varying knowledge and intent rather than a trusted experimenter, the IBT can be extended to probe how source credibility and other aspects of social cognition impact how learners integrate language [4].

text.text: More broadly, almost all tasks begin with instructions which participants hear or read and which set the frame for the current experiment, yet cognitive models almost universally do not model the instructions directly, PREPRINT instead assuming the model structure is in place already at the start of the task.
This work starts to push at the boundaries of what we include in our psychological accounts of such tasks.
We conducted two behavioral studies with samples recruited on Prolific (https://prolific.com/).
text.formatted: We conducted two behavioral studies with samples recruited on Prolific (<ref type="url" target="https://prolific.com/">https://prolific.com/</ref>).

text.text: Study 1 evaluated participants across all task and hint pairings in the IBT, surveying the space of scenarios in which language can influence experiential learning.

Study 2, designed to follow up on the findings of Study 1, manipulated the trial at which the hint appeared in order to test how accumulated experience changes the integration of linguistic information.
Neither study was preregistered, and all analyses are exploratory.
We recruited 340 participants in Study 1 and 300 in Study 2.
Participants self-reported their gender, which was not analyzed (Study 1: 176 men, 157 women, 3 preferred not to say, 1 other; Study 2: 140 men, 157 women, 2 preferred not to say, 1 other).
Sample sizes were not determined by an a priori power analysis.

A simulation-based sensitivity analysis (Section 4.6 and Appendix D) indicates that our design afforded 80% power to detect task-level hint effects of 2.1 to 10.6 percentage points of the arm spread depending on task.
Minimum detectable effects for individual hints ranged from 2.2 to 13.3 percentage points, and for individual hint-by-onset conditions in Study 2 from 3.8 to 8.9.
We filtered out any participants who did not complete all games (2 people) or failed the instruction comprehension quiz more than twice (1 person), leaving N=337 and N=300 for analysis, respectively.
We limited participation to adults from English-speaking countries (the US and UK) to ensure a baseline language competency.
Participants were aged 18 to 80 (mean 42.7) in Study 1 and 19 to 79 (mean 40.9) in Study 2.

We paid all participants at a rate of $15/hour with an additional bonus of up to $1.00, calculated proportionally to their performance in a randomly selected game trial (to avoid declining motivation later in the experiment).
Participants completed the experiment in a median of 12.4 minutes in Study 1 and 9.1 minutes in Study 2.
All procedures were approved by the NYU Institutional Review Board, and all participants provided informed consent before beginning the experiment.
In Study 1, participants played up to 15 games (see Appendix D for the composition of the Study 1 sample).
Each game was assigned a random configuration of task type and hint, sampled from our pre-defined IBT dataset.
In Study 2, each participant played 12 games.

Each game was assigned one of two task types: stationary, in which experience alone rapidly identifies the best arm, and the patch foraging task, in which the non-stationary reward structure makes experiential learning substantially harder.
This let us test the sensitivity of hint timing to task context while keeping the design tractable.
Each game was also assigned a hint timing parameter, which determined the trial (of [0, 4, 8, 12]) on which the hint would appear on the screen.
Both experiments used a within-subjects design, but because game conditions were assigned randomly, our analyses mix within-and between-participant comparisons.

In each game, participants were instructed to maximize their point earnings over 20 or 40 trials, depending on game type (two context, three context, and Bernoulli games had double the number of trials due to task complexity).
We kept the number of experiential trials relatively small in order to avoid overwhelming the information contributed by language.
The participants had to choose between 5 lettered buttons on the screen by clicking the buttons.
Each time they made a choice, their action and observed reward were logged in a running history table under the buttons, to reduce the load on memory.
In some games, a hint was provided at the top of the screen.

In Study 1, the hint was always present to the participant, and in Study 2, the hint was made visible only after a predetermined number of choices, altering the amount of prior experiential learning the subject had before being given a hint.

In the two context and three context cases, the participant also saw a shape (of circle, square, or triangle) on the screen at each trial to indicate which context they are in, and the context is additionally logged to the history table (Appendix H and Fig. A3).

text.text: An IBT learner should best estimate the means of the Gaussian arms in order to make optimal selections and maximize their expected rewards.
As rewards are noisy and observed only for the arm that was chosen, these estimates are inherently uncertain and built incrementally over trials.
One way to model these beliefs is with a Bayesian RL framework, where the learner's knowledge is represented as a probability distribution over the arm means and is updated after every trial.
Beyond providing a principled account of uncertainty, the Bayesian model allows for an additional language-informed prior to dually factor into the posterior belief.
At each timestep t, the learning agent chooses an action a t and observes a reward r t drawn from the taskspecific reward function.

The observation history is given by the full sequence of actions taken and rewards received, h t = (a 1 , r 1 , a 2 , r 2 , . . . , a t , r t ), and is sometimes annotated by additional contexts or features.
In the absence of language, RL is purely evaluative [2], and the only learning signal comes from these observed rewards.
text.formatted: In the absence of language, RL is purely evaluative <ref type="bibr" target="#b1">[2]</ref>, and the only learning signal comes from these observed rewards.

text.text: In this case, we can use Bayes' Rule to represent the agent's posterior distribution over the N arm means given h t as:
Under total uncertainty, the prior P 0 (µ 1:N ) is broad, and we use a Normal prior centered on the typical arm value (Appendix I).
In order to explore effectively, the agent must sample actions via Thompson sampling and iteratively update its beliefs to optimize the likelihood of the observations [14, 27].
text.formatted: In order to explore effectively, the agent must sample actions via Thompson sampling and iteratively update its beliefs to optimize the likelihood of the observations <ref type="bibr" target="#b13">[14,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b26">27]</ref>.

text.text: In both real world settings and in the IBT, however, the learner faces an additional challenge of determining which problem structure they are learning under before estimating the parameters of the problem.
We thus introduce a hierarchical Bayesian model which maintains uncertainty over both task types and parameters.

Letting τ ∈ {stationary, drifting, two context, three context, time delayed, patch foraging, Bernoulli, linear contextual} denote the task type and θ τ be the task specific parameters, the posterior of the hierarchical Bayesian model can be represented as:
The likelihood P (h t | τ, µ 1:N , θ τ ) encodes the generative model for each type.
We use closed-form conjugate updates (Normal-Normal for most of the tasks) to compute this term.
For types with unknown hyperparameters, the model uses Monte Carlo marginalization by sampling θ τ from the current type-specific priors and averaging over the resulting likelihoods.
After each trial, the hierarchical Bayesian agent updates its joint beliefs over task types and parameters, P (τ, θ τ | h t ).
Implementation details for each agent type are given in Appendix I. We additionally verify that the Bayesian hierarchical agent can correctly recover each of the task types in Appendix I and Fig. A4.
text.formatted: Implementation details for each agent type are given in Appendix I. We additionally verify that the Bayesian hierarchical agent can correctly recover each of the task types in Appendix I and Fig. <ref type="figure" target="#fig_3">A4</ref>.

text.text: To test which components of the agent account for its fit to human choices, we also fit ablated variants that drop the hint weight, replace the hierarchy over task types with a single stationary bandit, or fix the task type to its true value (Appendix G).
A key challenge is how to map the information from the natural language hints onto the learning problem.
As a motivating example, consider a learner given the hint "The value of arm 1 is greater than 25".

If the learner had first sampled arm 2 and observed a reward of 100, they would immediately recognize arm 2 to be a good choice, whereas if they had sampled arm 3 and received a reward of 0, they might be tempted to exploit arm 1 instead.
The key point being, information contained in the hint, combined with individual experience, can rapidly shift choice behavior.
Thus, we propose that the learning agent may use the information from the hint as a secondary Bayesian prior [21] [22] [23] to alter its beliefs over the task representations.
text.formatted: Thus, we propose that the learning agent may use the information from the hint as a secondary Bayesian prior <ref type="bibr" target="#b20">[21]</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b21">[22]</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b22">[23]</ref> to alter its beliefs over the task representations.

text.text: In particular, this term, representing the natural language information, should remain distinct from the prior over tasks and over parameters (these reflect something about the learner's understanding of the games or the world at large), combine with the observations, and additionally inform the posterior beliefs.
with estimating the mean of each of the N Gaussian distributions corresponding to the arms.
The parameter space that captures all possible arm mean configurations can then be defined as Θ = R N .
A natural language hint, l, places constraints on this space by essentially ruling out particular combinations of parameters from the possible worlds.

To capture the semantics (i.e., which possible worlds are retained or excluded given a hint), we construct a "semantic meaning function" f l , which is a mapping from the task parameterization to some real number indicating truth value [4, 28].
text.formatted: To capture the semantics (i.e., which possible worlds are retained or excluded given a hint), we construct a "semantic meaning function" f l , which is a mapping from the task parameterization to some real number indicating truth value <ref type="bibr" target="#b3">[4,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b27">28]</ref>.

text.text: More concretely, we define f l : Θ → R ≤0 ∪ {-∞}.

The extended real-valued functions allow us to capture categorically true or false hints, represented by 0 or -∞ respectively, as well as graded similarity judgments between parameter values in a manner analogous to fuzzy logic used in control engineering [29].
text.formatted: The extended real-valued functions allow us to capture categorically true or false hints, represented by 0 or -∞ respectively, as well as graded similarity judgments between parameter values in a manner analogous to fuzzy logic used in control engineering <ref type="bibr" target="#b28">[29]</ref>.

text.text: The meaning functions of the Bayesian model were fixed before Studies 1 and 2 were run.

While the first two examples in Fig. 2a visualize the weighting functions for value-based hints, other hints might weight the agent's belief over the task types (as in the third example), the sampled parameters, or the agent's action and reward history.
text.formatted: While the first two examples in Fig. <ref type="figure" target="#fig_1">2a</ref> visualize the weighting functions for value-based hints, other hints might weight the agent's belief over the task types (as in the third example), the sampled parameters, or the agent's action and reward history.

text.text: For example, a hint advising the agent to continue trying other arms throughout the game will use the trial time since the last selection of an arm as a weighting to upsample environments in which the best arm is one that the agent has not chosen recently.
In this way, all types of hints in the IBT dataset change the agent's likelihoods for selecting possible environments, thereby constraining the agent to only worlds consistent with the hint.

text.text: In equation ( 3), exp(γf l (τ, µ 1:N )) introduces the language dependency on the agent's posterior.
text.formatted: In equation ( <ref type="formula" target="#formula_3">3</ref>), exp(γf l (τ, µ 1:N )) introduces the language dependency on the agent's posterior.

text.text: The exponential maps the hint output (in (-∞, 0]) into the probabilistic space for compatibility, and γ adds flexibility to the model by allowing variation in the weight of language on the learning process.

Because hints that rule out possible worlds outright assign them a value of -∞, and hence a weight of 0 (and a value of 0, or a weight of 1, to those consistent with the hint), γ only changes the influence of soft hints, such as those that weight samples by the agent's choice history.

Algorithmically, the agent first computes the experienceonly posterior, samples a large batch of K hypothetical environments from this standard posterior and passes them through the meaning function to evaluate their compatibility with the linguistic hint.

Finally, the agent resamples a single environment from this weighted batch via importance sampling [30], selects the optimal action in that specific sampled environment with Thompson sampling [14], and executes the action to observe the next reward.
text.formatted: Finally, the agent resamples a single environment from this weighted batch via importance sampling <ref type="bibr" target="#b29">[30]</ref>, selects the optimal action in that specific sampled environment with Thompson sampling <ref type="bibr" target="#b13">[14]</ref>, and executes the action to observe the next reward.

text.text: Over the learning process, the agent maintains hierarchical beliefs to jointly infer task type and parameters.
The language-informed hierarchical Bayesian RL agent is able to model the optimal learner through all of the problems in the IBT.
In each scenario, the agent is provided no hint or one of the hints corresponding to the task type.
To assess whether state-of-the-art large language models harness the information from linguistic hints in sequential decision-making tasks, we evaluate variants of the Centaur model on IBT.
Centaur is a large language model fine-tuned on Psych-101, a large-scale dataset of past psychological experiments translated into text-based prompts [25].
text.formatted: Centaur is a large language model fine-tuned on Psych-101, a large-scale dataset of past psychological experiments translated into text-based prompts <ref type="bibr" target="#b24">[25]</ref>.

text.text: Psych-101 includes a number of multi-armed bandit experiments, so Centaur has been trained on human choices in related paradigms, but the IBT tasks and hints are not part of it.
The fine-tuning objective was to align the base model, Llama 3.1 70B [24], to human behavior by matching token likelihoods to human choices.
text.formatted: The fine-tuning objective was to align the base model, Llama 3.1 70B <ref type="bibr" target="#b23">[24]</ref>, to human behavior by matching token likelihoods to human choices.

text.text: One claim is that Centaur can predict human behavior for new behavioral tasks given only the relevant task instructions.
We were interested in evaluating it on IBT to carefully measure the impact that different hints would have on prediction behavior for a model that relies heavily on linguistic input.

We linearized our instructions and tasks following the protocol in [25], making only minimal changes to the text provided in the behavioral experiment to fit the query structure in the Psych-101 training dataset.
text.formatted: We linearized our instructions and tasks following the protocol in <ref type="bibr" target="#b24">[25]</ref>, making only minimal changes to the text provided in the behavioral experiment to fit the query structure in the Psych-101 training dataset.

text.text: To simulate each of the games, we iteratively passed as input the task instructions, trial relevant contexts, and history of past choices and rewards to the models.

We then extracted the predicted logits over the five valid action tokens (integers 1-5) and normalized via softmax (with generation temperature of 0.8 [25]) to obtain a probability distribution over the arm choices.
text.formatted: We then extracted the predicted logits over the five valid action tokens (integers 1-5) and normalized via softmax (with generation temperature of 0.8 <ref type="bibr" target="#b24">[25]</ref>) to obtain a probability distribution over the arm choices.

text.text: We ran the models on each task 100 times while randomly rotating the arm mean configuration to avoid numerical biases, then averaged the per-trial choice distributions across simulation runs to yield mean model probabilities for each task type, hint, and trial condition.
We fit each model to the choices of 337 participants using 5-fold cross-validation and a maximum-likelihood approach to compare how well each model accounts for human decision-making.
For the hierarchical Bayesian agent, we find the softmax temperature T and the weight of the linguistic hint γ which maximize the likelihood assigned to the true human choices at each trial.

First, we iteratively pass each action and reward from the human trials to the hierarchical Bayesian agent, simulate the belief update, then draw 500 weighted posterior samples over task type and parameters.
We then count the Thompson sampling actions across arms to construct a distribution over all actions.
For the language-informed hierarchical Bayesian agents, we additionally reweighted the posterior samples by the hint function raised to the power of γ to simulate the effect of the hint.
The reweighted action counts then pass through a softmax function with temperature T to produce the model's choice probabilities for that trial.
We precomputed these statistics for every trial, so that fitting T and γ required only closed-form likelihood evaluations over the cache.
We optimized both parameters using L-BFGS-B via the multivariate optimizer function scipy.optimize.minimize [31], with bounds T ∈ [0.1, 20.0], γ ∈ [0.1, 20.0].
text.formatted: We optimized both parameters using L-BFGS-B via the multivariate optimizer function scipy.optimize.minimize <ref type="bibr" target="#b30">[31]</ref>, with bounds T ∈ [0.1, 20.0], γ ∈ [0.1, 20.0].

text.text: In every fold, γ sat at its lower bound.

Refitting with the lower bound widened to 0.001 left T unchanged to two decimals and changed the held-out log-likelihood by at most 0.0002 nats per trial, so the bound does not affect the reported fits.

For Centaur, we introduced a rescaling parameter T that rescales the LLM's predicted choice distribution by a factor of β = T ref /T : P (a) = p(a) β a ′ p(a ′ ) β β > 1 sharpens and β < 1 flattens the rescaled probability distribution over action tokens.
text.formatted: For Centaur, we introduced a rescaling parameter T that rescales the LLM's predicted choice distribution by a factor of β = T ref /T : P (a) = p(a) β a ′ p(a ′ ) β β > 1 sharpens and β < 1 flattens the rescaled probability distribution over action tokens.

text.text: We fit β by extracting the choice probabilities at each trial of each game and scaling the distribution by this factor using the bounded scalar optimization function in Scipy (scipy.optimize.minimize scalar with bounds β ∈ [0.1, 20.0]).
We additionally fine-tuned Centaur on a training subset of the human bandit choices (Cen-taurIBT) using Low-Rank Adaptation (LoRA) by training with a cross-entropy loss over the five arm tokens.

Additional implementation details on fine-tuning as well as an analysis of how additional training sharpened the choice distributions are in Appendix F. Finally, we include a LLaMA baseline, the untuned Llama 3.1 70B model on which Centaur is built, scored on the same trials as Centaur, to isolate the contribution of Centaur's training on the Psych-101 dataset.
The latter two models were fit with the same temperature procedure as Centaur.
We evaluate all models on the held-out fold with the mean log-likelihood per trial, or the probability the model assigns to the human's actual choice (results in Section 2.4).
After the fitting procedure, we set the best-fit hint weight for the hierarchical Bayesian agent and temperature for Centaur and forward simulated each model to reproduce the behavioral dataset.
For the Bayesian model, we ran 100 independent agent simulations per MAB type and hint condition on freshly sampled bandit environments.

For Centaur, we prompted the model with the same text prompts used in the human task and sampled choices at each trial under the fitted temperature, yielding 100 simulated games per MAB type and hint condition.
We then analyze the hint effects of each of these datasets as compared to the behavioral dataset with the procedure in Section 4.5.2.
We use two complementary analyses matched to two questions.

Paired t-tests on early versus late trial regret verify that each task is learnable from experience alone, and linear mixed models, with participant random intercepts, estimate the task-level hint effects, the effect of each individual hint, and, in Study 2, how each effect changes with hint onset, while accounting for repeated measures and unequal games per condition.

To verify that participants learned within each task type from experience alone, we used only no-hint games and compared mean regret in the first five trials to mean regret in the last five trials using paired t-tests.

For each task type, we computed the average regret (the difference between the mean of the optimal arm and that of the chosen arm, expressed as a percentage of the game's arm spread) of the participants over these two windows.

A positive difference between mean regret in early and late trials indicates improvement over the course of the game. t : mean difference SE of difference is the difference relative to the variability.
We report two-sided p-values, adjusted with the Holm-Bonferroni procedure [32] across the eight tasks.
text.formatted: We report two-sided p-values, adjusted with the Holm-Bonferroni procedure <ref type="bibr" target="#b31">[32]</ref> across the eight tasks.

text.text: All eight human tests remain significant after correction.
Full results are in Appendix C.
We used a linear mixed model to quantify the effect of each hint on task performance for both humans and model simulations.

For people, we fit the model (neg regret ∼ hint + (1|subject)) separately for each task type to predict the negative mean per-trial regret, expressed as a percentage of the game's arm spread (higher is better) with hint condition as a fixed effect and with a participant random intercept to correct for individual variation.
Task-level hint effects were estimated with the same model, treating all hinted games as a single condition.
For the models, which lack individual variation, we fit the model (neg regret ∼ hint) by ordinary least squares with heteroscedasticity-robust standard errors.

For Study 2, the model was fit separately for each task type and hint onset, with both hinted and no-hint games restricted to post-onset trials and, at onsets 4, 8, and 12, the game's mean regret before the onset included as a covariate (there are no pre-onset trials at onset 0).
Each mixed model was estimated by restricted maximum likelihood using the statsmodels library [33].
text.formatted: Each mixed model was estimated by restricted maximum likelihood using the statsmodels library <ref type="bibr" target="#b32">[33]</ref>.

text.text: We report estimated differences, 95% confidence intervals, and two-sided p-values for each task type and hint combination.

The p-values are adjusted for multiple comparisons with the Benjamini-Hochberg false discovery rate procedure [34], applied separately to the 8 task-level effects, the 40 hint effects of Study 1, and the 40 hint-by-onset effects of Study 2.
text.formatted: The p-values are adjusted for multiple comparisons with the Benjamini-Hochberg false discovery rate procedure <ref type="bibr" target="#b33">[34]</ref>, applied separately to the 8 task-level effects, the 40 hint effects of Study 1, and the 40 hint-by-onset effects of Study 2.

text.text: Adjusted p-values and significance stars are reported for the human effects only.

To test whether hint effects in Study 2 depended on onset, we compared each hint's effect at trial 0 with its effect at each later onset (trials 4, 8, and 12) using a Wald test on the difference between the two estimates, and adjusted the 30 contrasts with the Benjamini-Hochberg procedure.
We draw upon this modeling framework throughout our behavioral analyses.

We conducted a simulation-based sensitivity analysis [35] to estimate the minimum detectable effect (MDE) [36, 37] of our experiment design at each level of inference reported in the paper: per-task aggregate hint effects (Fig. 3b), per-hint effects within task (Fig. 4), and per-timing effects in Study 2 (Fig. 5).

text.text: First, the two task types played by the largest share of participants (stationary and patch foraging) had the sharpest task-level resolution (MDEs of 2.1 and 2.3 percentage points of the arm spread), while the six task types assigned to participant subsets required larger effects (5.9 to 10.6 percentage points), with time delayed among the highest owing to its substantially larger residual variability (σ = 23.8).
Second, per-hint cells required correspondingly larger effects (MDEs of 2.2 to 13.3 percentage points across tasks), due to the smaller sample sizes per hint.
Third, Study 2's per-hint-by-onset cells had MDEs of 3.8 to 8.9 percentage points, and all five significant Study 2 effects exceeded their MDE.

Two of the four task-level effects reported as reliable in the main text exceeded their task's MDE, while two fell just below it (7.1 observed against an MDE of 7.4 for two context, and 10.4 against 10.6 for linear contextual), and we accordingly treat their magnitudes as approximate.

The MDEs also indicate that only large hint benefits were reliably detectable in the drifting, three context, and Bernoulli tasks, so the lack of aggregate hint effects (see Results in the main text) should not rule out the possibility of moderate effects.
At the per-hint level, 12 of the 13 significant effects (starred conditions in Fig. 4) exceeded their specific MDE.

Task-level MDEs ranged from 2.1 percentage points of the arm spread (stationary) to 10.6 (linear contextual), with the two tasks played by the largest share of participants (stationary and patch foraging) resulting in the sharpest resolutions (MDEs of 2.1 and 2.3) owing to their larger samples.
The per-hint MDEs ranged from 2.2 to 13.3, and per-hint-by-onset MDEs in Study 2 from 3.8 to 8.9.
Of the four task-level hint effects (reported in Section 2.1.1), two exceeded their task's MDE and two (two context and linear contextual) fell just below it.
At the per-hint level, 12 of the 13 effects meeting our reliability criterion exceeded their cell-specific MDE.
The remaining one was detected despite falling below it, and we treat its magnitude as approximate (Appendix D).

To ensure our findings generalize beyond any single problem structure, we constructed the Instructed Bandit Tasks (IBT) to span a wide array of bandit variants commonly studied in the reinforcement learning and cognitive science literature.
The eight task types were chosen to systematically vary the computational demands placed on the learner.

Each task type admits a different family of linguistic hints about its underlying structure, making the set well suited for studying how instructions interact with qualitatively different learning problems.

text.text: The Study 1 sample combines two batches.
In the first, 159 participants each played 15 games, each assigned a random configuration of task type and hint sampled from the pre-defined IBT dataset.

The second comprises 178 participants who completed the first build of the Study 2 experiment, in which every hint appeared at trial 0; we included their games with hints from the Study 1 hint set (10 per participant, all stationary or patch foraging).
Because Study 2 drew its trial-0 conditions from the same sessions, 74 of these participants also contribute games to Study 2, and 740 games appear in both datasets.

We computed MDEs at three levels, namely (a) task-level aggregate hint effects (Fig. 3b; 8 cells), (b) per-hint effects within task (Fig. 4; 40 cells), and (c) per-hint effects at each onset in Study 2 (Fig. 5; 40 cells).

We analyzed each synthetic dataset with the same mixed model and recorded whether the hint effect was detected (criterion below).

To assess fine-grained behavioral alignment between models and human participants, we computed three metrics from the sequence of arm choices a 1 , a 2 , . . . , a T over a game of T trials.
Switch Rate Switch rate measures the proportion of trials on which the agent changed its choice relative to the previous trial: where 1[•] is the indicator function.
Higher values indicate more exploratory behavior.

Choice Entropy Choice entropy measures the uniformity of arm selection over the full game using the Shannon entropy of the empirical choice distribution: where K is the number of arms and pk = 1 T T t=1 1[a t = k] is the empirical frequency of arm k across trials.
Higher entropy indicates more uniform exploration across arms.

Exploitation Onset Exploitation onset measures how early an agent committed to a single arm, defined as the normalized trial index of the first occurrence of five consecutive identical arm choices: We fine-tuned Llama-3.1-Centaur-70B [25] on human bandit choices using Low-Rank Adaptation (LoRA) [49], implemented via Unsloth with 4-bit quantization.
text.formatted: Exploitation Onset Exploitation onset measures how early an agent committed to a single arm, defined as the normalized trial index of the first occurrence of five consecutive identical arm choices: We fine-tuned Llama-3.1-Centaur-70B <ref type="bibr" target="#b24">[25]</ref> on human bandit choices using Low-Rank Adaptation (LoRA) <ref type="bibr" target="#b48">[49]</ref>, implemented via Unsloth with 4-bit quantization.

text.text: The model was loaded in 4-bit and adapted with LoRA applied to all attention and MLP projection matrices, with rank r = 16, α = 16, and dropout = 0.05.

Fine-tuning followed the same participant-level 5-fold cross-validation as the other models (Methods, main text): in each fold, the model was fine-tuned on the training participants (about 269) and evaluated on the held-out participants (about 68), so that no participant's choices appeared in both.
At each trial, the full game history up to that point was formatted into the same prompt used during simulation, and the model was trained to predict the human's next arm choice.

Rather than standard cross-entropy over the full vocabulary, we used a choice-restricted loss, where logits were extracted only for the five arm-choice tokens, and label smoothing (ϵ = 0.05) was applied to prevent overconfidence.

We fine-tuned Centaur for 2 epochs with AdamW (lr = 2 × 10 -5 , weight decay = 0.01), batch size 4 with gradient accumulation over 2 steps (effective batch size 8), gradient clipping at 1.0, and a cosine learning rate schedule with a 5% linear warm-up.
Maximum sequence length was 1,024 tokens.
Hyperparameter choices were largely set to default.
Fine-tuning was run on a single NVIDIA H200 GPU with 128 GB of host memory and was allocated a 12-hour wall-time limit on an HPC cluster node.
Fig. A1 shows the rank-ordered average choice probability for the base Centaur model and the fine-tuned CentaurIBT model.

text.text: We observe that fine-tuning on IBT sharpens the distribution.
CentaurIBT concentrates 88.6% of probability mass on the top-ranked arm on average, as compared to the 79.0% for base Centaur.
This overconfidence is the primary reason that CentaurIBT under-performs across IBT tasks in Fig. 7a.
text.formatted: This overconfidence is the primary reason that CentaurIBT under-performs across IBT tasks in Fig. <ref type="figure">7a</ref>.

text.text: When the model's top-ranked arm does not match the human choice, the log-likelihood is severely penalized as the probability mass is low on all other arms.
This indicates that either higher label smoothing or entropy regularization may be required during fine-tuning in order to improve model prediction.
We asked which components of the Bayesian model account for its fit to human choices and for its predicted hint effects.
To do so, we fit ablated variants of the model with the same five-fold cross-validation and fitting procedure as the full model (Methods, main text), changing only the ablated component.
• No hint.
Drops the hint weight from equation (3) entirely, including for hard hints, and fits only the softmax temperature.
The agent learns from experience alone.
• Non-hierarchical.
Replaces the hypothesis space of eight task types with a single stationary bandit.

Value and history hints still act on the sampled arm means, but hints about the task type or about parameters a stationary bandit lacks (e.g., the delay or the linear-contextual features) have no effect.
• Fixed type.
Gives the agent the true task type, so it infers only the parameters within that type.
Hints that act only on the task type have no effect.
• Shuffled hint.
A control for the content of each hint.
Each hinted game is scored with the meaning function of a different hint from the same task, one the participant did not see but that is still true of the game.
We cycled through each task's hint list, giving four shuffled variants.
Held-out negative log-likelihood is averaged over the eight tasks with equal weight, because stationary and patch foraging have about twice as many participants as the other tasks.
(Averaged over trials instead, as in the main text, the full model's value is 1.300 nats per trial.)
Differences between variants are tested with paired t-tests over participants.
Because the task-weighted means and the per-participant differences weight the data differently, the gap between two task-weighted means need not equal the mean per-participant difference.
In every hinted variant, the hint weight γ sat at its lower bound of 0.1 in all five folds.
This is expected: γ scales only the soft, history-based hints (Methods, main text), and the fit prefers them as weak as allowed.
Widening the bound to 0.001 gave γ = 0.001 in every fold, left T unchanged to two decimals, and changed the held-out negative log-likelihood by at most 0.0002 nats per trial.
The bound is therefore immaterial.
First, we find that language accounts for most of the fit (Fig. A2).
text.formatted: First, we find that language accounts for most of the fit (Fig. <ref type="figure">A2</ref>).

text.text: Removing the hint weight raised the heldout negative log-likelihood from 1.315 to 1.403 nats per trial (per-participant difference 0.11 [0.10, 0.12], p < .001).
text.formatted: Removing the hint weight raised the heldout negative log-likelihood from 1.315 to 1.403 nats per trial (per-participant difference 0.11 [0.10, 0.12], p < .001).

text.text: The hint-blind model also predicted no hint effects: its correlation with the human per-hint effects was r = 0.09, against 0.73 for the full model.
Next, we verified that hint benefits depend on their task content.

Scoring games with a different, still-true hint from the same task fit almost as poorly as no hint (1.383-1.391 nats), and the predicted hint effects no longer tracked those of people (r between -0.25 and 0.25).
Removing the hierarchy cost very little overall (1.346 nats; per-participant difference 0.007 [-0.001, 0.015], p = .086), but this near-zero difference hides two opposing effects.

The hierarchy fit choices better in tasks whose structure a stationary learner cannot represent (three context, time delayed, and linear contextual) and worse in tasks that people treated as simple bandits (Bernoulli, drifting, and patch foraging), where uncertainty over task type made the agent explore more than people did.

Without the hierarchy, model correlation with human effects also dropped from 0.87 to 0.05 for policy hints and from 0.43 to 0.12 for structure hints, while the correlation for value hints did not drop (0.49 and 0.67).
Finally, the skyline Bayesian model is task-specific.

In this case, giving the agent the true task type indeed improved fit (1.306 nats; per-participant difference 0.011 [0.008, 0.014], p < .001) and the correlation with human hint effects (r = 0.79), at the cost that hints acting only on the task type have no effect.
