The hierarchical model maintains a posterior P (τ, θ τ | h t ) over eight task types.
Each type implements a conjugate or Monte Carlo likelihood.
All types use a shared Normal-Normal arm mean prior with µ0 = 45, σ0 = 20, which approximates the mean and spread of the given arm values.
Stationary The agent runs a closed-form Normal-Normal update.

At each trial t, the predictive variance for arm a is σ 2 a + σ 2 obs,a , where σ 2 a is the current posterior variance of arm a's mean, and σ 2 obs,a is the known observation noise, which is set to the bandit arm's standard deviation.
After observing reward r, the posterior precision is updated as λ ′ a = λ a + 1/σ 2 obs,a and the mean as µ ′ a = (µ a λ a + r/σ 2 obs,a )/λ ′ a .

Drifting For drifting bandits, the agent uses a Kalman filtering framework [40] to track non-stationary means by marginalizing over a distribution of drift rates ϵ ∼ N (µ ϵ , σ 2 ϵ ) (prior µ ϵ = 2, σ ϵ = 1) and growing the posterior variance by the sampled ϵ 2 at each timestep to enforce a recency bias on observations.
text.formatted: Drifting For drifting bandits, the agent uses a Kalman filtering framework <ref type="bibr" target="#b39">[40]</ref> to track non-stationary means by marginalizing over a distribution of drift rates ϵ ∼ N (µ ϵ , σ 2 ϵ ) (prior µ ϵ = 2, σ ϵ = 1) and growing the posterior variance by the sampled ϵ 2 at each timestep to enforce a recency bias on observations.

text.text: The log marginal likelihood is estimated via Monte Carlo over 10 sampled ϵ values.
The posterior belief over ϵ is updated via importance-weighted moment matching on the samples.
The agent maintains a categorical distribution over delay values k ∈ {1, 2, 3, 4, 5} with uniform prior.
For each candidate k, it computes the Normal-Normal log marginal likelihood by pairing each observed reward at trial t with the action taken at trial t -k.
The posterior P (k | h t ) is updated via Bayes' rule.

The agent models a deterministic transition where arm means deplete when chosen and replenish otherwise by marginalizing over a change rate λ ∼ N (µ λ , σ 2 λ ) with prior µ λ = 0.2, σ λ = 0.08, using 40 Monte Carlo samples.

After observing a chosen arm a, its mean is multiplied by e -λ and all other arms are multiplied by e +λ , capped at a running estimate of each arm's equilibrium mean, updated online from observations.
The posterior over λ is again updated via importance-weighted moment matching.
Two context and three context The agent maintains independent Normal-Normal arm mean posteriors for each context (2 or 3, respectively).
Only the beliefs associated with the current context index (provided as side information from the trial history) are updated at each trial.
The log marginal likelihood sums over context-appropriate observations only.
Bernoulli For Bernoulli bandits, the agent performs a Beta-Bernoulli conjugate update to estimate the success probabilities of each arm, with prior Beta(α 0 , β 0 ) = Beta(1, 1) per arm.
Rewards are in {0, 100}, and any other observed reward sets the log likelihood to -∞, falsifying the Bernoulli hypothesis.
Wins increment α a , and losses increment β a.
Finally, for the linear contextual bandits, the posterior is a multivariate normal over the weights of the linear model.
The agent performs standard Bayesian linear regression [50] to maintain a covariance matrix for the 3-dimensional features, with a Gaussian prior θ ∼ N (0, 100I).
text.formatted: The agent performs standard Bayesian linear regression <ref type="bibr" target="#b49">[50]</ref> to maintain a covariance matrix for the 3-dimensional features, with a Gaussian prior θ ∼ N (0, 100I).

text.text: After each trial, the posterior is updated in closed form from the observed feature and reward pairs.
The expected reward for an arm is then the dot product of its features with the sampled weights.

After computing log likelihoods ℓ τ = log P (h t | τ ) for each type, the type posterior is updated as: with uniform prior P (τ ) = 1/8 at t = 0, using log-sum-exp normalization for numerical stability.
The agent uses Thompson sampling to select actions.
At each trial, K = 500 samples (τ (i) , µ (i) 1:N , θ (i) τ ) are drawn from the current posterior P (τ, µ 1:N , θ τ | h t ).
When a hint l is present, each sample is reweighted by: where f l is the hint meaning function defined in the Methods of the main text and γ is the fitted hint strength parameter.

A single hypothesis is then resampled from this weighted population (or uniformly if no hint) via importance sampling [30], and the agent's action is the greedy arm, a (i) = arg max a µ (i) a , of that resampled hypothesis.
text.formatted: A single hypothesis is then resampled from this weighted population (or uniformly if no hint) via importance sampling <ref type="bibr" target="#b29">[30]</ref>, and the agent's action is the greedy arm, a (i) = arg max a µ (i) a , of that resampled hypothesis.

text.text: The resulting reward is observed and the trial data (a, r) is appended to the history h t before the next belief update.

We conducted a type recovery analysis using the actual parameters from the behavioral experiment (five arms with means [10, 20, 40, 60, 80] and σ = 5) to assess whether the hierarchical Bayesian agent can correctly identify which of the eight task types it is observing.
text.formatted: We conducted a type recovery analysis using the actual parameters from the behavioral experiment (five arms with means <ref type="bibr" target="#b9">[10,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b19">20,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b39">40,</ref> <ref type="bibr">60,</ref> <ref type="bibr">80]</ref> and σ = 5) to assess whether the hierarchical Bayesian agent can correctly identify which of the eight task types it is observing.

text.text: For each task, we simulated 20 independent games using a random policy.
After observing the full sequence of actions and rewards for each game, we performed a single batch belief update and recorded the agent's posterior P (type | data) across the eight candidate types.
We averaged the agent's posteriors across the 20 repetitions per type.
Fig. A4 shows the resulting confusion matrix.
text.formatted: Fig. <ref type="figure" target="#fig_10">A4</ref> shows the resulting confusion matrix.

text.text: Each row corresponds to the true task type used to generate the data, and each column corresponds to the agent's posterior belief of a given type.
Four task types, Bernoulli, two context, three context, and linear contextual, are identified with near-perfect accuracy.
Time delayed yielded strong posteriors (0.92).
The agent was moderately confused between stationary and drifting as expected.
With only 20 trials and a drift rate of ε = 2, the reward variance attributable to drift is small relative to observation noise, making the two distributions nearly indistinguishable.
Finally, patch foraging is the most difficult to identify (0.46 correct), with residual mass split between stationary (0.25) and drifting (0.27).
This is justified by the fact that depletion and replenishment signals are extremely difficult to detect under random exploration, as they require arms to be chosen repeatedly.

Overall, the analysis confirms that the agent is well-calibrated for the structurally distinctive task types and that confusions are confined to the tasks that are genuinely hard to distinguish from random-policy observations.
Figure1.
The Instructed Bandit Tasks and modeling approach. a) Participants see a hint and their reward history in the IBT task interface.
Centaur, a language model fine-tuned on human behavior, receives the same task instructions, hint, and history as text.
The Bayesian model combines the hint with priors over task types (τ ), arm means (µ) and taskspecific parameters (θ), and updates its beliefs after each choice and reward.

This paradigm yields choice trajectories for all three learners under each task condition. b) The three learners are compared on the effect on performance for each hint, hint effects based on timing, choice patterns, and fit to held-out human choices.
Figure 2.

Formalizing language in the Bayesian model. a) Each linguistic hint translates into a logical meaning function f , which operates over the parameter space of the problem. exp(γf ) then gives a probabilistic weighting over sampled parameter configurations.
Two toy value hints weight the arm means µ1 and µ2 (left, center).

A structure hint weights the task type τ , here placing equal weight on the two task types with contexts (right). b) One simulated three context game with and without the hint "The button values change under each shape."
The top row plots beliefs computed from the observations alone, and the bottom plots those reweighted by the hint.
The bold line is the true type. c) The resulting action distributions for the same simulated three context game, with (bottom) and without (top) the hint.
The dashed line marks chance, and the color strip along the bottom of each plot shows context changes over the trials.
Figure3.

Humans learn in each task and hints improve performance on most task types. a) Trial-by-trial regret (as a percentage of the game's arm spread, where 0% is always choosing the best arm and 100% the worst), averaged across participants for no-hint games (purple), generally decreases over trials for every task type.
The Bayesian model (teal) and Centaur (orange) simulations are overlaid.

Shaded regions are ±1 SEM. b) Per-type hint advantage for humans and both models, computed as the difference in mean regret between no-hint and hint games, in percentage points of the arm spread (positive values mean hints benefit).
Error bars are 95% confidence intervals from a linear mixed model for people and from ordinary least squares with robust standard errors for the models (Section 4.5.2).

Hint effects vary by hint and task type for both humans and models.

Humans integrate hints differently depending on prior experience. a) Average trial-by-trial regret of participants in Study 2 for the stationary (solid) and patch foraging (dashed) tasks, with markers at the four hint onsets (trials 0, 4, 8, and 12).
Shaded regions are 95% confidence intervals across participants. b) Human hint effects for all 40 hint-by-onset conditions, as the normalized regret reduction relative to the no-hint baseline.

text.text: Figure6.
Centaur best reproduces patterns in human choice trajectories.
Each panel shows a scatter plot of the condition-level means (48 points, one per task type and hint condition) for human participants (x-axis) versus the model simulated trajectories (y-axis).

The three columns separately plot switch rate (the fraction of trials on which the agent changed its arm selection), choice entropy (the Shannon entropy of the empirical arm selection distribution over the full game), and exploitation onset (the normalized trial index of the first run of five consecutive identical choices), and the rows correspond to the Bayesian model and Centaur.
The points are colored by task type.
The dashed diagonal visualizes y = x, and the Pearson r values are shown in each panel to measure correlation agreement (n = 48 conditions, all p < .001).
